On the 22nd of August, Judge Robinson issued a new decision that -- to the effect that those two lists were put under seal, and that was done only on the 22nd of August. And in this decision by Judge Robinson there is a quote where it is said that the Prosecution has not explicitly stated that these documents were confidential and under seal. I believe that we did submit this, that we tendered this decision, so I thought really that I was not violating any orders. And it was absolutely not my intention to commit contempt of court in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the key issue. Did you publish, where did you publish, and when did you publish this?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: I published the list, if I remember correctly, on the internet page www.domagojmargetic.com. That was on the 23rd of July this year. So 12 days after the decision that made me -- led me to believe that this list was in fact the public Exhibit number 18. And the decision that -- that followed on the 22nd of August indicates that there had been some confusion even in the minds of Judges. There probably was some kind of a clerical confusion within the Tribunal itself which caused this decision to be actually issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: Domagoj, did you give any statements or interviews to HINA news agency either on the 1st of August or on the 2nd of August or on any other date before or after that one regarding the publication?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: The only statement that I gave to my colleagues is I informed them that I had been summoned to the county court in Zagreb where I was to accept service of an order from a Judge of the Tribunal, and I told them that I would come to the court to accept service. And I definitely did not give an interview to the HINA news agency. I did give an interview the next day or the next night to Vecernji List newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not give an interview to HINA.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: No. I only gave an interview to a journalist from Vecernji List daily newspaper. And I think it was actually published in Croatia that was -- that was published on the 5th of August, which is the day of homeland thanksgiving and the day of victory. It was the holiday issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: After you were in placed in detention by the county court in Zagreb, were you informed about the measures that were taken or the orders that were issued by this Tribunal to prevent you from publishing the list, the confidential information, and if yes, what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: When I learned that I had to come to the county court pursuant to their summons, I was at the seaside, and I travelled from the coast to Zagreb in order to heed the summons from the county court in Zagreb, and then there was this story launched by the journalists, and my colleagues told me that this summons -- that the summons actually pertained to an order issued by the Tribunal regarding the protected witnesses. So they cooked up this story. And as soon as I arrived in Zagreb, I removed the list of protected witnesses from my web site, because at that moment it became clear to me that the decision of the 11th of July that there was something amiss with it. Before I actually came to the court, that was on the morning of the 4th of August, at 9.00, I -- that's when I came to the county court, and before that I had already removed the list from my web site, and I actually said that to the judge of the county court in Zagreb, in my testimony, and she was able to satisfy herself that really this was removed from my web site, that the list was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the detention unit of the county court in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, in the afternoon, that's -- I was arrested, and I would like to let the Judges of the Tribunal know that the -- that the order issued by this Tribunal was in fact abused, in a way, to such an end that I was in the end arrested as a common criminal in my own country. I reported to the police in Slavonski Brod myself because I was on my way to Vukovar where I was supposed to do some publicity for a book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, you asked about the length of the detention. I missed, as a matter of fact, the relevance of that issue at this moment in this case. The witness is now explaining further, going in quite some details. I would like you either to guide him to a point of relevance or to move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't think that he would go into so many details. The purpose of my question was the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: Domagoj, can you please tell the Judges whether you expressed your readiness to accept service of any orders issued by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify something for you, Your Honours. At no time did I refuse to take service of the -- any of the orders of the Tribunal. This is an untruth, and this was told the Tribunal by the Croatian authorities. I tried to calm the situation down in Zagreb through the president of the Croatian Helsinki Committee but to no avail. I merely wanted the county court in Zagreb to abide by its own procedure as it does in all other cases, and I said I will take service, take receipt of this order just as I had before from the Tribunal. Every time I came to the county court I took receipt of all the documents served on me. And this is -- you have written proof of that at the county court. Despite that, they informed the Tribunal that I had refused to take receipt of the order, which is completely untrue. And after I ended up in detention, I wrote the Tribunal because I wanted to make -- make it clear that I did not want to be responsible of contempt of court, that I -- I merely wanted to apologise and to promise that I will not do that again, because I was misled. I had been misled by the decision published on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: One of my last questions, or indeed the last question perhaps: Did you have any intent to commit contempt of court and, if not, what was your intent when you published this list?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: After I was led to believe by the decision of the 11th of July that this list was in fact the public exhibit number 18, as an investigative journalist I of course went through the names on this list, and I compared this to not only some documents originating from Bosnia and Herzegovina but also from the international community, and I discovered that four witnesses from this list were at the same time listed as suspects, participants of various terrorist organisations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is an area that I am interested in, a book I -- I published a book quite recently about Islamic terrorism in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in south-east Europe, and it is dealing with those terrorist organisations that infiltrated Bosnia and Herzegovina over the past 15 years and participated in the war there. As an investigative journalist, once I was led to believe that this was the list that was made public as a public exhibit number 18, it was interesting to me to discover that protected witnesses called by the Prosecution are at the same time suspected of participating in terrorist organisations by some other organisations. It was also my intent to prove that one witness who is not a protected witness anymore had actually given false testimony before this Tribunal. This was Stjepan Mesic, Mr. Stjepan Mesic, who was a protected within before this Tribunal. In one of the trials, which was the Blaskic trial, as he testified and as he was asked by the Trial Chamber whether he knew the name of at least one soldier that participated in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and was forced to do so, in other words, that was forcibly mobilised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, I think the issue at this moment is whether it was protected material, yes or no. If it was protected material, then for whatever motive, to please his neighbours or to do a favour to anyone else, that is not the reasons of publication. It may have some impact perhaps on sentencing if someone is found guilty, but apart from that not relevant. Mr. Margetic has clearly explained to us at this moment that he feels that it's his duty as an investigative journalist to give expression to what kind of witnesses are protected in this Tribunal. He seems to be of the opinion that many of them should not be protected. That's difficult to judge upon if you do not know why they are protected witnesses, but let's leave it for that. Further details on why witnesses should not have been protected are at this moment not relevant. It's clearly understood what Mr. Margetic moved when he published the material. Please proceed. It was your last question you said before. Is that -- Mr. Margetic, if you would like to finish your answer but without going into details on whether Witness X, Y, or Z would properly be protected or not. It's finally this court who decides that and not the investigative journalist. Is there anything else you'd like to add to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I put in the most important thing, and this is the fact that from the period of the 11th of July to the 22nd of August I believed this document to be in the public domain, and that is the main reason why I published it, because I was convinced that in this period, 11th of July, 22nd of August, I believe that list to be the public exhibit number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions. I have to admit that I myself did not know where this question would take my witness, but this is my last question. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness, I would have one question to clarify. You said you learned about what you call the 11th of July decision mid-July on the internet. Do you remember on what web site you found that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the link was mentioned in our pre-trial brief, if I'm not mistaken, but I think it was either one of the web sites of the Tribunal or a web site that was in some way linked with the Tribunal web site. Your Honour, I know that the -- that I reached this material when I was looking for all the materials relevant for the trial of my colleague Mr. Jovic on the internet. So when I searched the internet for that I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now your answer is a bit ambiguous. You start saying that you found it on the web sites of the Tribunal. You said either of the two, or at least a web site linked to the Tribunal, and finally now you say, "I found it somewhere on the internet." Now, what -- could you be more precise in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the exact link is provided in our pre-trial brief. I don't know it by heart, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would say, "In our pre-trial brief I stated," then Mr. Miljevic is invited to review the pre-trial brief so that the Chamber could be informed about where exactly to find the reference to the internet site where Mr. Margetic found the -- what he calls the 11th of July decision. Mr. Margetic, what is in your pre-trial brief is not evidence. Therefore, I asked you, but I now do understand that you say, "It's written down in our pre-trial brief, and that's what I remember to be correct." Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Prosecution has an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. And perhaps as some guidance there is quite some material now in evidence which gives, to say the least, a different impression of what Mr. Margetic had on his mind when he published the list. The Chamber is aware of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated earlier in your evidence that you did not receive the letter of the 6th of April from the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown -- can the accused be shown Exhibit 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you say you didn't receive that letter?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: No. I really never received a letter like this. I saw a quote from this letter being mentioned in the indictment, but I never received a letter such as this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And before you received the Rule 65 ter -- sorry, before you received the supporting material in this case on the 13th of October, you'd never seen that letter before?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown a document, please, a new document, and if it can be marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit. I think it's number 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's leave it in the hands of Madam Registrar. She's very accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 32, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, this is an e-mail from you sent on the 10th of January, 2006, to a number of different recipients. That e-mail address, that's an e-mail address that you regularly use?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown another document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be document 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, again the -- it's an e-mail from you dated the 17th of March, 2006, to a number of different recipients, again from your web site; is that correct -- your e-mail address?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is the -- the text of the document is in B/C/S, but we don't seek to tender it for the contents of the document, simply for the e-mail address at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then we assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's number -- Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 33. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Margetic, if this is -- looking at the next document, which is an e-mail from you on the 20th of April, 2004, again from your regular e-mail address to a number of recipients?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness -- the accused be shown another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we now have three documents to identify what seems to be the e-mail address of Mr. Margetic. I take it you will not present another five, six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more, about the content or just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any dispute about this being the e-mail address used by Mr. Margetic, as was said before, or is there any time issue involved?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd rather this one also be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think I was clear that as far as matters stand now, both the evidence Mr. Margetic gave and the three documents at least give a good suspicion for accepting that this is Mr. Margetic's e-mail address.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And next document I wish to show him is a very crucial e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the last document is marked Exhibit 34?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, madam --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that will be Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the next document is an e-mail address -- an e-mail from Sebastiaan van Hooydonk on the 3rd of April, 2006, to you at your domagojmargetic@yahoo.com e-mail address which you have advised the Court that that was your regular address. The e-mail reads: "Dear Mr. Margetic, please find attached a letter from Mr. Akerson re disclosure of 65 ter exhibits. Stop. The hard copy of this letter and the CD containing the material will be sent to you today. Kind regards, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, ICTY OTP/TSU," and then the address of the Tribunal and the telephone number.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I haven't finished my -- I was simply setting out what the e-mail content was about. And attached to this e-mail was the letter dated the 6th of April, 2006, which was addressed to counsel for Mr. Jovic, counsel for Mr. Krizic, counsel for Mr. Seselj, and yourself. This is the same copy of Exhibit number 3 which is in this case. The letter is from David Akerson, Office of the Prosecutor, and it says: "Please find enclosed Rule 65 ter exhibits and translations that are additional to the previous to the 1st December, 2005 disclosure. If you have any questions about any of this, please don't hesitate to contact me directly. "Again, this material is subject to oral and written non-disclosure orders. None of this material is to be used or disclosed for any purpose not directly related to the preparation and presentation of the above-titled cases. It may not be used for any other purpose --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there really a need to read it again? I mean, it's the same document as is already in evidence. We are very limited in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. The question, of course, Mr. Margetic, is did you receive this document by e-mail as an attachment to the -- the e-mail shown to you, addressed to your e-mail address? Did you receive it as an e-mail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The first time I set eyes on this document was when I arrived at the Tribunal. I have no reason to tell anything but the truth about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is clear. You said you didn't receive it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 18, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We really are on very serious time restraints. The Chamber is even considering to make closing arguments a written exercise rather than in court because we have to stop in no more than 20 minutes from now on. There's another trial which has to continue in this courtroom. Yes. Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, that Vecernji List newspaper article says that you got the list from Mr. Akerson, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Akerson was in charge of the last case against Croatian journalists on behalf of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The picture of the CD in that Exhibit 18 shows -- shows a copy of the CD, and you've also mentioned earlier today that it had the case number and a Rule 65 ter disclosure. So how do you know that you got the material from Mr. Akerson if you didn't receive that letter with the warning that the material was -- contained orders for non-disclosure?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: As I pointed out before, Mr. Akerson was the senior trial attorney on behalf of the OTP in the last case against Croatian journalists, and he submitted to us all the materials that were related to the proceedings and the trial. He and no one else. That was the only logical conclusion that I was able to draw. If I'd had that particular letter, don't you think that instead of a scanned surface of a CD it would have been the list? I simply didn't have the list. When I arrived at the Tribunal was the first time I set eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I put it to you you're lying and you did receive the letter.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Erroneously, if I may say. I'm really sorry, but could I please ask you to try and not insult me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You knew the list was confidential when you published it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Not true. I pointed out to the Trial Chamber what my position was regarding the publishing of that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were so convinced that the list was public because of this purported 11 July 2006 order, which no one has been able to locate, then why did you define it in your articles as a confidential list if you were convinced that the list was public?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: It had been confidential. You know, we journalists always apply a certain method when we write about something, when we discover something when, we publish a document that used to be confidential up until a short time before, if we're dealing with state secrets, it is a secret because, de facto, the first time it's published is when journalists get hold of it, and then a state body allows for it to be published. This is a very common MO among us journalists. That's how we write and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does "MO" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, right up until the 12th of September you were still referring to this as a confidential list, secret list, protected witnesses list. You knew that it was protected. You knew that it was confidential, and you disclosed this document in knowing violation of Tribunal orders.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: That is simply not true. That's what I'm telling you. When a document is published, that's what journalists do. If you look at American journalism, you have cases like that all the time. The secret services disclose a document after 20 years. The editors and journalists publish that document which is now in the public domain because the state says so, and then the journalists describe it as a secret FBI document, for example, or a secret document coming from the judiciary and so on and so forth. It used to be a classified document but now a state body has allowed for this document to suddenly become public so you have journalists publishing it. It's just how journalists work and how they tackle their topics. I explained my motives in great detail and with the utmost sincerity. I thought the list was public Exhibit number 18 dated the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so all the --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: The 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- protective measures that were contained on that witness list, you thought all -- that the Tribunal had lifted all orders in relation to all 48 witnesses, did you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding. That was my understanding of the document I found on the internet. And it follows, doesn't it? If you look at the ruling dated the 20th of August, it is clear that there was some sort of a mistake, and I wasn't the only one making it. The Tribunal was making it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is interested in facts, not in whether they are logical or not. Sometimes facts are not logical. Sometimes they are. Please proceed. That's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, there is no 11 July decision in relation to this witness list, and I put it to you that you're lying. You know -- you knew that the document was confidential when you published it. You knew that the witnesses were protected, and you published it because you wanted to do it. You wanted to out all of these witnesses who testified against the Croat General Tihomir Blaskic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: That is entirely erroneous. I don't even know Mr. Blaskic personally. Therefore, your suggesting that I would do that is entirely erroneous. You're entirely off the mark. Why would I have done that? Could you at least explain why I would have waited for two months in that case? If what you're suggesting is true, I would have published the list in May. I wouldn't be waiting for July, in fact until past the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that you waited until days after the indictment against you was withdrawn. Knowing that there was no indictment hanging over your head you thought, Well, let's go out and publish the witness list today. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: But that is just not true. The indictment against me was withdrawn nearly two months after I received the list, or a month later possibly. That is just untrue. How could I possibly have known that the indictment would be withdrawn in June?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic --

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Nobody could have known. I was taken aback by that particular piece of news.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's my point. You got the information on the 6th of April. You were told it was confidential. You waited until the indictment against you was withdrawn on the 20th of June, 2006, and then within days thereafter you published the witness list on the web site.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Madam, that is just not true. What I told you was the truth. I told you exactly what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say that the reason why you -- you published this list was because you wanted people to know the truth. You wanted people to know that these witnesses had given false testimony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: The job of any journalist is to write the truth. That's what I believe. As I started saying a while ago, I proved that a particular witness of the OTP was no longer a protected witness, Mr. Stjepan Mesic, as a then protected witness of the OTP gave evidence to this international court and to the international public that was simply false, and judgements were later based on his evidence, important ones at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Let's talk about Mr. Mesic's evidence. How did you know it was false testimony? Did you read it, the Blaskic testimony?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: Do you think I have enough time to explain to you why I knew that his evidence was perjury, in fact. It wouldn't take longer than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question was: Did you read Mr. Mesic's Blaskic testimony, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: What you're asking me is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: -- how I knew that Mr. Mesic was lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, the question was whether you have read the testimony of Mr. Mesic in the Blaskic case. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I cross-referenced it with the Milosevic case evidence, and I realised that in one of those two trials Mesic was in fact lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who provided with you a copy of Mr. Mesic's Blaskic testimony?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: As you probably know, the first to publish the evidence of Mr. Mesic at the Tribunal were the Tribunal people themselves, but then they subsequently removed this document from their page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, would you please answer the questions. The question was: Who provided you a copy of the Mesic testimony in Blaskic? Simple question. Simple answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evidence that Mr. Mesic gave in the Blaskic case was one of the documents that could be accessed on a Serbian web page, an agency called Veritas, led by Mr. Savo Strbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is did you receive it from there or did you receive it from anywhere else? It's not where it was accessible but where you got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only did I obtain Mesic's evidence in that way but also a whole lot of other foreign journalists. I believe a number of British journalists wrote about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was closed session testimony. How did you know there was other false testimony of the other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did I know? Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, whether or not the witness takes the position that it was false testimony in this case we'll not be able -- and it might not be that relevant whether it's for the full hundred per cent truth. So therefore, unless you could explain what is the relevance, I said before that the reasons why are not that important. It's mainly what has been done or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this issue goes to Rule 77(A)(iv), the interference with the witnesses. If I can just have a few questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is we have eight minutes left for the whole of the day, or we'll have to adjourn again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljevic, would you have any additional questions as far as matters stand at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have asked all the questions that I meant to ask. The accused at one point started deviating from the subject of his book, so the last thing I wanted to ask him if in his trial brief he also enclosed his own book and whether there was an English translation. That's the only thing I forgot at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. I'll strictly keep you to that then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can answer my questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can answer my questions and keep your answers brief I would appreciate it very much. Can you explain to the Court how you were able to tell which of the 48 witnesses gave false evidence?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: The same as the reasoning applies as in the case of Mr. Mesic. I cross-referenced their evidence before the Court. Most of this was in open session, so we as journalists can cross-reference their testimony, much like you do. We check it for consistency about one and the same circumstance or, if, rather, they were beating about the bush and talking nonsense instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By looking at names on that witness list, how could you tell that they provided false testimony simply by their names, apart from Mr. Mesic, who you've already discussed?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: The question regards circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I've been following that over a long period of time, and I've written pieces about it. I have a whole network of people informing me about what goes on in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was much in the same way that I found out that certain people had cooperated with the Bosnian intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, simple question. Did you have sound reasons and, if so, where did you get them that the 48 witnesses, or at least the over 40 witnesses with a protected status, at least at a time, whether they were all lying, whether they were all false witnesses? The question is quite simple. Is it that you say Mr. Mesic lied and therefore we have to expose this because the others may have lied, or do you have information about the others lying in court, the others who enjoyed protective measures? For all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. My first motive was not to publish a list that was protected. I thought it was a public list. Secondly, I had reliable, serious information that those witnesses had been proved by the Bosnian intelligence services and that special briefings had been done to guide them in terms of their testimony, evidence, and lies before this Tribunal. These are serious matters that I'm telling you. My information was reliable and serious and the matter is indeed very serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Margetic, in your official statement, which is Exhibit 25, you state the reason why you published the witness list in part was to reveal to the world that some witnesses were in fact Mujahedin or better known to the world as terrorists. "In light of the anniversary of 9/11, it is important that the public to know with whom the ICTY were working with to prosecute Blaskic." You wanted to single those people out, didn't you, for the fact they testified against Blaskic. You didn't care what repercussions became for any of those witnesses, did you?

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: This is completely untrue, madam. I am a Catholic, and I care deeply for all human beings, and as a religious person I cannot disregard the fate of other people. The fate of every human being is important to me, and here you're completely in the wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In an accompanying article to the witness list, you stated that you would sooner or later publish the confidential document because you have done before. You would always do it regardless of the people in question. You didn't care. You wanted -- you wanted to put this witness list out there because you wanted to single these people out.

utterances.speaker: DOMAGOJ MARGETIC
utterances.text: This is simply not true, madam. The reasons why I published this list were presented by me several times here. A journalist has certain responsibility once he or she obtains certain documents, and I have already told the Trial Chamber that I have absolutely no intention of publishing any documents originating from this Tribunal, public or confidential, and I promised the Trial Chamber that I will abide by the order that was issued by -- by His Honour Judge Orie, and I in fact did that. I complied with all the orders issued by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I gave you five minutes. These five minutes are gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Miljevic, you said you had no further questions. You had forgotten one question in the first round, although re-examination is not there to put questions you forgot to put in the first round. Therefore, I take it that the cross-examination didn't raise any issue on which you'd like to further examine the witness. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of respect for the Tribunal, I said that I forgot, but in fact you, Your Honour, intervened when my client moved from his book on Islamic terrorism to Stjepan Mesic, and this is why I did not insist on the matter, and I didn't ask what I had originally intended, in other words, whether this book was published, whether it was translated into English, and whether it was in fact appended to the pre-trial brief. So this is just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you let this issue go? If so, then Mr. Margetic should take his place again, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the Trial Chamber did its utmost best -- what I didn't say is that if so then you would have to move. We are not there yet, Mr. Margetic, but remain for a second where you are at this moment. The Trial Chamber thinks that it's inappropriate now to try to finalise this in such a hurry that the -- that the Trial Chamber would feel that time became more important than truth. Therefore, the Trial Chamber decides that we'll adjourn for the day. We'll find another date where we'll finalise the examination of Mr. Margetic as a witness, where perhaps additional questions will be put to him by the Bench, where, Mr. Miljevic, the question we found no time for today may be put to him if that would not go too far beyond what can be done in re-examination, of course I do not know exactly what it is. So therefore we'll have to take more time to conclude this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we are adjourning at time-limits as imposed also on the Prosecution would then be reconsidered as well. There's one issue, however. Usually if an accused takes the stand he is not allowed to have contact with counsel when his testimony has not been finished yet. Should we apply that rule in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In our submission yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miljevic, there is a rule which is usually applied that someone who has taken the stand should not consult with counsel up till the moment that he finished his testimony. Are you aware of this rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am aware of this rule, and I can abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there's no objection this rule to be applied. Of course then we'll try to adjourn -- to seek another day as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask the Chamber to make a -- give the accused a warning that he should not publish anything to do with these proceedings between now and when he comes back for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Margetic already nodding yes. Mr. Margetic, could you confirm that you will not, even without an order of the Chamber, that there's a commitment that you will not publish anything? That would be the only reason why the Court would not give you an order. Yes. Your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I undertake not to discuss the proceedings in any way, and you can see that I have not published anything about the Tribunal or the proceedings in my blog, and I have absolutely no intention of discussing the proceedings with anyone. I will comply fully with the order that I have already received from you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then well understood. The Chamber will consider and inquire into when this trial could be finished. It might not take very long the next session, perhaps one or two hours. It has the advantage that we can hear oral final argument by the parties, which is preferred by this Chamber above written final argument. We stand adjourned sine die.
